::: {.lead}
Every cave of *Torch Hall* is different: the walls, the coins, the bats and
the loot come from random numbers. But the testers report strange things:
all five bats fly the same way, the "daily challenge" is different for two
friends on the same day, and a legendary sword drops far too often. A
computer cannot roll a real die: it **computes** numbers that only look
random. In lectures 13 and 14 you computed probabilities. In this lesson you
see how a **pseudo-random generator** works, what a **seed** is, how random
numbers become dice, lanes and critical hits, and how to **shape** them: a
**uniform** distribution and a **weighted** choice with a loot table. Every
section ends with a short task.
:::

## Key terms

{{< glossary pseudo-random-number prng lcg modulo seed procedural-generation probability-distribution uniform-distribution weighted-random cumulative-weight loot-table histogram >}}

## 15.1 Why games need random numbers

Chance makes games surprising and replayable: different levels, loot,
enemy behaviour and critical hits (@fig-pseudo).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 15.1 — Pseudo-random numbers"}
**Real chance** comes from the physical world: a die, noise, the exact time
between key presses. A computer usually makes **pseudo-random numbers**
with a fixed formula, a **pseudo-random number generator (PRNG)**: each
number is computed from the one before. They look random and pass
statistical tests, but the same start always gives the same numbers.
:::

![Real chance and pseudo-random numbers.](images/pseudo-random.png){#fig-pseudo width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 15.1 — Chance in Torch Hall"}
1. **Procedural generation:** the walls and coins of each cave.
2. **Loot:** the item in each chest (the crates of lecture 14).
3. **Behaviour:** the direction in which a bat flies next.
4. **Combat:** a critical hit with probability 0.2.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Thinking that pseudo-random means "not random enough for games". For
games, a good PRNG is ideal: fast, and repeatable when you need it. (For
passwords and online money, special secure generators are used.)
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Find the chance"}
Choose a game you play. Write four things in it that come from random
numbers.

*Your result:* a list of four.

::: {.check}
A good list names four different things, for example the map of a level,
the item in a chest, where an enemy moves next, and a critical hit. Check:
each one changes from game to game without the player choosing it.
:::
:::

## 15.2 A generator by hand: one LCG step

One of the oldest generators fits in one line. You only need to follow one
or two steps by hand to see the idea (@fig-lcg).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 15.2 — Linear congruential generator"}
An **LCG** computes
$$x_{n+1} = (a \cdot x_n + c) \bmod m.$$
**mod** (modulo) is the remainder of a division: 38 mod 16 = 6. All values
are between 0 and m − 1. The first value x₀ is the **seed**. Because there
are only m values, the sequence repeats; the number of values before the
repeat is the **period**, at most m.
:::

![An LCG by hand with a = 5, c = 3, m = 16 and seed 7.](images/lcg-steps.png){#fig-lcg width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 15.2 — Seed 7"}
a = 5, c = 3, m = 16, x₀ = 7:

1. x₁ = (5·7 + 3) mod 16 = 38 mod 16 = **6**.
2. x₂ = (5·6 + 3) mod 16 = 33 mod 16 = **1**; x₃ = 8 mod 16 = **8**.
3. Step by step, the numbers 7, 6, 1, 8, … look random, but after 16
   numbers 7 comes again: the period is **16**.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Writing your own generator "for fun" in a real game. Small m gives short
periods and patterns. Use the generator of the engine or of the language.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · By hand"}
With a = 3, c = 1, m = 8 and seed 2, compute the next two numbers.

*Your result:* two numbers.

::: {.check}
x₁ = (3·2 + 1) mod 8 = 7 mod 8 = **7**; x₂ = (3·7 + 1) mod 8 = 22 mod 8 =
**6**.
:::
:::

## 15.3 Seeds: the same start, the same numbers

The seed is the key to repeatable randomness (@fig-seeds).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 15.3 — Seed"}
The **seed** is the start value of a PRNG. The **same seed gives the same
sequence**, and so the same level, loot and events. A game chooses the
seed:

- from the **time** or the system: a new game every time;
- from a **number** the player types or shares: the same world for friends;
- from the **date**: a daily challenge, the same for all players today;
- **saved** with the inputs: an exact replay, and bugs that can be repeated.
:::

![The same seed gives the same level.](images/seeds.png){#fig-seeds width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 15.3 — The daily cave"}
1. The seed is the date as a number: 25 October 2026 → **20261025**.
2. Every player who opens the daily cave today builds it with this seed:
   the same walls, coins and bats for all.
3. Tomorrow the seed is 20261026: a new cave for everybody.
:::

{{< sim file="sims/seed-lab.html" poster="sims/seed-lab.png" title="Seed Lab: the same seed, the same level" height="680" >}}

::: {.callout-caution title="In game code"}
```csharp
// Unity: one generator for the level, seeded once.
var rng = new System.Random(seed);          // seed = 20261025 for the daily cave
for (int i = 0; i < cells.Length; i++)
    cells[i] = rng.NextDouble() < 0.22 ? Cell.Wall : Cell.Floor;
```
:::

**Seed once.** A game makes one generator when the level starts and keeps
asking it for the next number. If the code seeds again and again (for
example in every frame, with the time), it gets the same first number many
times.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 15.4 — The five bats"}
Every bat seeds the generator with `Time.time` in each frame. In one frame
the time is the same for all five bats, so every bat gets the same seed and
the same first number: all bats fly the same way. Fix: seed once when the
level starts.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Seeding from the time when players should share a world. Two friends start a
second apart and get different caves. Use a shared number or the date.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Seeds"}
In **Seed Lab**, build seed 42 twice, then 43. Then press Daily challenge.
Write what stays the same and what changes.

*Your result:* three short notes.

::: {.check}
Seed 42 twice gives exactly the same level. Seed 43 gives a different level.
Daily challenge uses today's date as the seed: every player gets the same
level today, and a new one tomorrow.
:::
:::

## 15.4 From random numbers to game values

A PRNG gives numbers in a fixed range. The game needs dice, lanes, items
and yes/no decisions (@fig-range).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 15.4 — Scaling random numbers"}
From a number r with 0 ≤ r < 1:

- an integer from **min** to **max − 1**: floor(r · (max − min)) + min;
- yes with probability p: **r < p**;
- a value between a and b: a + r · (b − a).

In Unity, **Random.Range(min, max)** with integers gives min … max − 1 (the
max is **not** included); with floats, the max can be included.
**Random.value** gives a float from 0 to 1.
:::

![From a random number to a die.](images/range-map.png){#fig-range width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 15.5 — Dice, lanes and critical hits"}
1. A die: `Random.Range(1, 7)` → 1 … 6.
2. Three lanes numbered 0, 1, 2: `Random.Range(0, 3)`.
3. A critical hit with p = 0.2: `if (Random.value < 0.2f) Crit();`.
4. A coin bonus between 5 and 15 (float): `5 + Random.value * 10`.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
`Random.Range(1, 6)` for a die: the 6 never comes, because the max of the
integer version is not included.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Write the call"}
Write the call for: (a) a card from 52 cards (0 … 51); (b) a lane 1, 2 or 3;
(c) a miss with probability 0.15.

*Your result:* three lines of code.

::: {.check}
(a) `Random.Range(0, 52)`; (b) `Random.Range(1, 4)`; (c)
`if (Random.value < 0.15f) Miss();`. The integer max is not included.
:::
:::

## 15.5 Distributions: is every value equally likely?

A random variable can take many values. Its **distribution** says how
likely each value is.

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 15.5 — Distribution and histogram"}
The **probability distribution** of a random variable lists every value with
its probability; the probabilities add up to 1. A **histogram** shows how
often each value came in many tries; with many tries it looks like the
distribution (lecture 13).
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Example 15.6 — Two distributions"}
1. One die: values 1 … 6, each with probability 1/6.
2. A chest: common 0.6, rare 0.3, epic 0.09, legendary 0.01. Sum: 1.
3. After 1000 chests the histogram shows about 600, 300, 90 and 10.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Judging a distribution from 20 tries. Small samples jump a lot; use hundreds
or thousands of tries before you decide that something is wrong.
:::

The simplest distribution gives every value the same chance (@fig-uniform).

In a **uniform distribution** every value is equally likely. **Discrete:** n
values, each with probability 1/n (`Random.Range(0, n)`). **Continuous:**
every number in a range is equally likely (`Random.Range(0f, 10f)`); the
chance to land in a part of the range is proportional to its length.

![A uniform distribution.](images/uniform.png){#fig-uniform width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 15.7 — A random spawn time"}
A bat appears after `Random.Range(2f, 6f)` seconds. P(the bat comes in the
first second of the range, from 2 to 3) = 1/4, because 1 s is a quarter of the
4-second range.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Using a uniform choice when the design wants rare items. With four rarities,
uniform means 25 % legendary: rarity needs weights.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Uniform chances"}
(a) `Random.Range(0, 8)`: P(5)? (b) `Random.Range(0f, 10f)`: P(the value is
from 7 to 10)? (c) Why is P(exactly 7.000…) zero in (b)?

*Your result:* three answers.

::: {.check}
(a) 8 values, so 1/8. (b) The part from 7 to 10 is 3 of the 10 units: 3/10.
(c) One exact point has no length in the range, so its chance is 0; only a
part of the range has a chance.
:::
:::

## 15.6 Weighted random choice

Most loot in games is **weighted**: each option has a weight, and heavier
options come more often (@fig-weighted).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 15.6 — Weighted choice"}
Each option i has a **weight** wᵢ ≥ 0. Its probability is
$$P(i) = \frac{w_i}{w_1 + w_2 + \dots + w_n}.$$
To pick: compute the **cumulative weights**, draw r uniformly from 0 to the
sum, and take the first option whose cumulative weight is greater than r. A
**loot table** is such a list of items and weights.
:::

![Weighted choice with cumulative weights.](images/weighted.png){#fig-weighted width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 15.8 — A chest of Torch Hall"}
Weights 60, 30, 9, 1 (sum 100); cumulative 60, 90, 99, 100.

1. r = 72: the first cumulative value above 72 is 90 → **rare**.
2. r = 99.4: above 99 → **legendary** (the bar from 99 to 100).
3. P(epic) = 9/100. With weights 3 and 1, P = 3/4 and 1/4: the sum does not
   need to be 100.
:::

::: {.callout-caution title="In game code"}
```csharp
int PickWeighted(int[] w) {
    int sum = 0; foreach (int x in w) sum += x;
    float r = Random.value * sum;          // 0 … sum
    int acc = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < w.Length; i++) {
        acc += w[i];
        if (r < acc) return i;             // first cumulative value above r
    }
    for (int i = w.Length - 1; i >= 0; i--)
        if (w[i] > 0) return i;            // r == sum (Random.value can be 1)
    return -1;                             // all weights are 0
}
```
:::

{{< sim file="sims/loot-table-lab.html" poster="sims/loot-table-lab.png" title="Loot Table Lab: weights and chances" height="740" >}}

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Using `r <= acc` with a weight of 0: an item with weight 0 can then drop when
r lands exactly on its border. Use `r < acc`, so weight 0 means "never".
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · A loot table"}
1. In **Loot Table Lab**, open 1000 chests and compare the counts.
2. Make epic items 5 % of the drops, and write your weights.

*Your result:* a count and a set of weights.

::: {.check}
After 1000 chests the counts are close to 600, 300, 90 and 10. For epic
5 %, for example weights 60, 34, 5, 1 (sum 100): 5/100 = 5 %.
:::
:::

## Case study: Loot Forge

The loot designer of *Torch Hall* has six questions. A chest has the loot
table common 50, rare 35, epic 12, legendary 3. A rack holds a bow with
weight 2 and an axe with weight 3. The cumulative weights of the chest are
50, 85, 97, 100, and the random number is r = 90. A critical hit should come
with 15 %. The daily cave must be the same for all players. And one item has
the weight 0. The Game challenge of the interactive page uses these
questions. In the mini-game below you answer them.

{{< sim file="sims/loot-forge.html" poster="sims/loot-forge.png" title="Loot Forge: shape the randomness" kind="game" height="440" >}}

Randomness Techniques for Game AI".

## Exercises

1. What is the difference between real chance and pseudo-random numbers?
2. Compute 23 mod 5 and 40 mod 8.
3. With a = 5, c = 3, m = 16, what follows x = 12?
4. What does the seed decide?
5. Why does a daily challenge use the date as the seed?
6. Why should the generator be seeded only once?
7. Which numbers does Random.Range(0, 10) give?
8. Write a call for a die with 8 faces (1 … 8).
9. How do you make a yes with probability 0.3 from Random.value?
10. What must the probabilities of a distribution add up to?
11. Random.Range(0f, 20f): P(the value is less than 5)?
12. Weights 5, 3, 2: the three probabilities?
13. Cumulative weights 40, 70, 95, 100 and r = 71: which option?
14. Which weight makes an option impossible?

## Answers to the exercises

::: {.answers}
1. Real chance cannot be repeated; pseudo-random numbers come from a formula
   and the same seed repeats them.
2. 3; 0.
3. (5·12 + 3) mod 16 = 63 mod 16 = 15.
4. Where the sequence starts, and so all the numbers that follow.
5. All players get the same level today, and a new one tomorrow.
6. Seeding again, for example with the same time, repeats the same numbers.
7. 0 … 9.
8. Random.Range(1, 9).
9. Random.value < 0.3f.
10. 1.
11. 5/20 = 1/4.
12. 5/10, 3/10, 2/10.
13. The third option (70 ≤ 71 < 95).
14. 0.
:::
